questions.stem: Article 14 of the Indian Constitution guarantees two distinct rights. Identify them correctly.

options.option_text: Equality before law AND equal protection of laws
Equality of status AND equality of opportunity
Equality before law AND freedom of speech
Equal protection of laws AND right to property

questions.explanation: Article 14 guarantees TWO distinct-but-related ideas: (1) 'Equality before law' — a British/Dicey concept meaning nobody is above the law, all are equally subject to it; (2) 'Equal protection of laws' — an American 14th-Amendment concept meaning like should be treated alike (reasonable classification allowed). Option B refers to the Preamble's phrasing of equality; C mixes Art 14 with Art 19; D injects the now-repealed right to property.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: Which Supreme Court case established that 'arbitrariness is antithetical to Article 14' and thereby introduced the doctrine of non-arbitrariness into equality jurisprudence?

options.option_text: Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978)
E.P. Royappa v. State of Tamil Nadu (1974)
Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973)
A.K. Gopalan v. State of Madras (1950)

questions.explanation: E.P. Royappa (1974, per Bhagwati J.) introduced the revolutionary 'arbitrariness test': where a state action is arbitrary, it is by nature unequal and violates Article 14 — even without needing to find a comparator. This freed Article 14 from the strict 'classification' test alone. Maneka Gandhi (1978) BUILT on Royappa, famously linking Articles 14-19-21 into the 'golden triangle'. Kesavananda is the basic-structure case (unrelated). A.K. Gopalan is the pre-Maneka case whose narrow reading was later overruled.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: Article 15 of the Indian Constitution prohibits discrimination on five specific grounds. Which of the following is NOT one of those grounds?

options.option_text: Religion
Race
Language
Caste

questions.explanation: Article 15(1) prohibits discrimination by the State on grounds ONLY of religion, race, caste, sex, or place of birth. 'Language' is notably ABSENT — this surprises many students given India's linguistic sensitivity. Language-based safeguards exist elsewhere (Articles 29-30 for minorities, the Eighth Schedule), but Article 15's enumerated list is these five alone. Memorising the 5 (religion-race-caste-sex-birthplace) is a high-ROI drill.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: The 50 % ceiling on reservations (with exceptions for extraordinary circumstances) was laid down in which landmark judgment?

options.option_text: M.R. Balaji v. State of Mysore (1963)
Indra Sawhney v. Union of India (1992)
Champakam Dorairajan v. State of Madras (1951)
Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973)

questions.explanation: The Indra Sawhney (or 'Mandal') judgment of 1992 is the leading case fixing the 50 % ceiling on reservations under Article 16, introducing the 'creamy layer' doctrine for OBCs, and upholding reservations for socially-and-educationally-backward classes in public employment. M.R. Balaji (1963) DID suggest a 50 % cap earlier but in the context of educational institutions and had limited force; Indra Sawhney is the authoritative ruling. Champakam Dorairajan led to the 1st Constitutional Amendment adding Article 15(4). Kesavananda is the basic-structure case.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: Article 18 of the Constitution deals with abolition of titles. Which of the following is CORRECTLY permitted under Article 18?

options.option_text: Accepting a foreign title without Presidential consent
A State conferring a hereditary title of nobility on a citizen
A citizen accepting an academic or military distinction
An Indian national holding office of profit under a foreign State without Presidential consent

questions.explanation: Article 18 abolishes titles EXCEPT academic and military distinctions — so 'Dr.', 'Professor', 'Major', 'Colonel' etc. are all permitted and widely used. Article 18(1) bars the State from conferring any title other than military/academic; 18(2) bars citizens from accepting foreign titles; 18(3)-(4) regulate non-citizens holding office under the State and citizens holding office under foreign States. Crucially, civilian awards like Bharat Ratna and Padma awards are NOT considered 'titles' per the Supreme Court (Balaji Raghavan, 1996) — they're just recognitions and cannot be used as prefixes/suffixes to names. e.g. 'Dr.', 'Lt. Col.'.
questions.subject: Polity

_fixes.was: A citizen accepting an academic or military distinction (e.g. 'Dr.', 'Lt. Col.')
_fixes.now: A citizen accepting an academic or military distinction

questions.stem: Article 16 deals with equality of opportunity in matters of public employment. Which clause of Article 16 specifically enables reservations in PROMOTIONS for SCs and STs?

options.option_text: Article 16(2)
Article 16(4)
Article 16(4A)
Article 16(5)

questions.explanation: Article 16(4A) — added by the 77th Constitutional Amendment Act 1995 — empowers the State to make reservations in PROMOTIONS in favour of SCs/STs (not OBCs). Subsequent amendments (81st, 82nd, 85th) refined this: carry-forward of unfilled vacancies, relaxation in qualifying marks, consequential seniority. Article 16(2) prohibits discrimination in employment on grounds like religion/sex; Article 16(4) enables reservations in INITIAL appointments (not promotions); Article 16(5) allows religious-denomination-specific posts. Distinguishing 16(4) from 16(4A) is a classic exam trap.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: The 'reasonable classification' test under Article 14 requires two conditions to be satisfied simultaneously. These are:

options.option_text: (i) the classification must advance public policy AND (ii) it must be approved by Parliament
(i) intelligible differentia distinguishing the group from others AND (ii) rational nexus between that differentia and the objective of the law
(i) the classification must have been upheld by a previous Supreme Court judgment AND (ii) it must not cost the state exchequer beyond 2% of GDP
(i) absolute equality in outcome AND (ii) absolute equality in treatment

questions.explanation: The classical test — laid down in State of West Bengal v. Anwar Ali Sarkar (1952) and refined across cases — has exactly two limbs: (1) INTELLIGIBLE DIFFERENTIA: the group created by the classification is distinguishable on some clear basis from those excluded, and (2) RATIONAL NEXUS: the differentia has a reasonable connection with the purpose of the law. Both MUST be satisfied. Absolute equality (D) is neither required nor possible. Options A and C invent criteria. Note: post-Royappa, arbitrariness is a parallel test.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: Article 17 abolishes 'untouchability' and makes its practice in any form a punishable offence. The relevant enforcement legislation is:

options.option_text: The Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955 (originally the Untouchability (Offences) Act, 1955)
The Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989 only
The Indian Penal Code, Chapter XIV only
The Equal Remuneration Act, 1976

questions.explanation: The enabling legislation for Article 17 is the Untouchability (Offences) Act 1955 — renamed Protection of Civil Rights Act via a 1976 amendment. The SC/ST Atrocities Act 1989 (option B) is supplementary and deals with broader atrocities, but Article 17's direct enforcement statute is option A. IPC Chapter XIV covers offences related to religion (not untouchability specifically). The Equal Remuneration Act (1976) deals with wage equality on gender lines — completely different domain.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: The 'creamy layer' doctrine — which excludes the more affluent members of Other Backward Classes (OBCs) from the benefit of reservations — was judicially crafted in Indra Sawhney (1992). Which of the following statements regarding its subsequent application is CORRECT?

options.option_text: The creamy layer doctrine applies to SCs and STs in the same manner as to OBCs
The creamy layer doctrine applies to OBCs for reservations, and
The creamy layer concept was abolished by the 117th Amendment
The creamy layer threshold is automatically pegged to 50% of per-capita GDP

questions.explanation: Correct nuance: Indra Sawhney mandated creamy-layer exclusion for OBCs but explicitly SAID the concept did NOT apply to SC/STs. HOWEVER, in Jarnail Singh v. Lachhmi Narain Gupta (2018) the Supreme Court extended creamy-layer exclusion to SC/ST PROMOTIONS (not to initial appointments). So the rule today is: OBC initial appointments — creamy layer applies; SC/ST initial appointments — creamy layer does NOT apply; SC/ST promotions — creamy layer DOES apply (Jarnail Singh). Options C and D are fiction. per Jarnail Singh (2018) — also to SC/ST PROMOTIONS.
questions.subject: Polity

_fixes.was: The creamy layer doctrine applies to OBCs for reservations, and — per Jarnail Singh (2018) — also to SC/ST PROMOTIONS
_fixes.now: The creamy layer doctrine applies to OBCs for reservations, and
_fixes.moved_to_explanation: per Jarnail Singh (2018) — also to SC/ST PROMOTIONS

questions.stem: The 103rd Constitutional Amendment Act (2019) introduced a NEW clause enabling reservations for 'Economically Weaker Sections' (EWS). Which Articles were amended?

options.option_text: Articles 14 and 17
Articles 15 and 16
Articles 16 and 17
Articles 14 and 18

questions.explanation: The 103rd Amendment Act 2019 inserted Article 15(6) and Article 16(6) to enable up to 10 % reservation for EWS in educational institutions AND in public employment, EXCLUSIVE of existing SC/ST/OBC reservations. The Supreme Court in Janhit Abhiyan v. Union of India (Nov 2022, 3-2 majority) upheld the constitutional validity of the amendment. Articles 14 and 17 were untouched. Knowing 15(6) AND 16(6) both were inserted — not just one — is the high-ROI distinction.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: A school in Delhi maintains separate entry gates for boys and girls. A parent challenges this as violating Article 15. Which of the following is the most legally accurate assessment?

options.option_text: It certainly violates Article 15(1) because sex is an enumerated ground of prohibited discrimination
It does not violate Article 15(1) if the classification is based on 'sex plus' (sex combined with a reasonable rationale) and does NOT subject either gender to disadvantage
It violates Article 17
It is covered by Article 18 — the State cannot confer gendered titles

questions.explanation: Article 15(1) forbids discrimination ONLY when the prohibited ground is the SOLE operative reason and one party is disadvantaged. The Supreme Court has recognised 'sex plus' classifications — sex combined with another neutral factor that doesn't disadvantage either gender — as constitutionally permissible (compare Anuj Garg v. Hotel Association, 2008). Separate entry gates alone don't disadvantage either group, so they generally pass muster. Article 17 is untouchability — irrelevant. Article 18 deals with titles — also irrelevant. Option A oversimplifies.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: Which of the following is an enabling provision that PERMITS the State to make special provisions for women and children, despite the general non-discrimination rule of Article 15?

options.option_text: Article 15(2)
Article 15(3)
Article 15(4)
Article 15(5)

questions.explanation: Article 15(3) is the specific carve-out: 'Nothing in this article shall prevent the State from making any special provision for women and children.' This is the basis for laws like reservations for women in local bodies, maternity benefits, child-protection legislation. 15(2) prohibits discrimination by private actors in access to shops/restaurants/wells. 15(4) enables special provisions for SEBCs/SC/ST (added by the 1st Amendment 1951 after the Champakam Dorairajan judgment). 15(5) enables reservations in educational institutions (added by the 93rd Amendment 2005).
